title: Bleeding an hour after birth

bedside.infusions: Oxytocin: {oxyUp ? "increased per protocol" : "maintenance rate"}. Second IV: {secondIv|yesno}. Bladder: {bladderFull ? "full" : "emptied"}.

banner.text: The obstetric hemorrhage team is at the bedside.

objective: Recognize postpartum hemorrhage -- cumulative blood loss of 1,000 mL or more within 24 hours of birth, by either route -- measure blood loss quantitatively, and activate the hemorrhage team
secondaryObjectives: Postpartum care, and assessing for hemorrhage and infection
Assess the postpartum fundus and bladder: a boggy uterus displaced above the umbilicus and to one side often means a full bladder, so help the client empty it and massage the fundus
Intervening on circulatory complications: hemorrhage, embolus, shock
Assessing and responding to changes and trends in vital signs
Recognizing a trend in the client's condition and intervening on it

sources.note: Relayed from the REQ-233 NCLEX-RN cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read: Physiological Adaptation includes managing a medical emergency and recognizing changes in vital signs; Reduction of Risk Potential includes monitoring for signs of bleeding.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

sources.note: Read 2026-11-14 (summarizing fetch with quotes): ACOG redefined PPH as cumulative blood loss over 1000 mL, or blood loss with signs and symptoms of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of birth by any route; uterine atony is the most common cause; rapid assessment, bimanual massage with uterotonics and ample IV access; methylergonovine 'is contraindicated in patients with hypertension'; carboprost may cause bronchospasm in asthma; tachycardia and hypotension may be masked in postpartum women, so a large loss can sit behind normal vital signs. Re-read directly 2026-11-16 (summarizing fetch with quotes): the point-of-care page still says of methylergonovine 'It is contraindicated in patients with hypertension' and that 'tachycardia and hypotension may be masked'; the NCBI Bookshelf edition of the same chapter (NBK499988; Wormer, Jamil and Bryant; updated 2024-07-19) says it 'is relatively contraindicated in patients with hypertension' and words the ACOG definition as loss 'with signs and symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours of the birth process'.

sources.note: Read 2026-11-14 (summarizing fetch with quotes): oxytocin first line (30 units in 500 mL; 10 units IM if no IV); methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM every 2-4 h, contraindicated with hypertension, preeclampsia or heart disease; carboprost 250 mcg IM every 15-90 min, maximum 2 mg, contraindicated with asthma or cardiac, renal or hepatic disease; misoprostol 400 mcg sublingual or 1000 mcg rectal. brief.situation: 15:00 on a labor and delivery unit. Ms. Morgan, 31, gave birth vaginally at 14:00 to a 4.2 kg baby after an 18-hour oxytocin induction. Her gestational hypertension ran 140s-150s/90s in labor. The baby is skin to skin. She says she feels 'a gush' and a little dizzy.
handover: Delivery blood loss was weighed at 300 mL; she has soaked pads since. Oxytocin is running at the maintenance rate. She has asthma as a child, none since. One 18-gauge IV.

The unit's hemorrhage protocol: weigh pads and linen for quantified blood loss (QBL); fundal massage; empty the bladder; the nurse may increase oxytocin per protocol; activate the hemorrhage team at a QBL of 500 mL or more with ongoing bleeding; methylergonovine is in the hemorrhage kit.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
The bleeding goes on while you work. Some steps take a few minutes.
Partway through you are asked to write what is happening and why. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What is happening, what makes it a hemorrhage rather than normal lochia, and what do you do first, next and why?

parts.label: Recognition
parts.criteria: Names postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony: a boggy fundus displaced up and to the right by a full bladder, heavy bleeding with clots, a weighed (not eyeballed) blood loss rising past 500 mL toward 1000 mL, HR rising while BP still looks normal because postpartum vital signs mask loss; risk factors of a big baby and a long oxytocin induction.
parts.modelAnswer: This is a postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony: the fundus is boggy and pushed up and to the right by a full bladder, she is passing clots, and the weighed loss is past 500 mL and climbing. Her HR is rising while her BP still looks fine, which is how postpartum women hide blood loss. A 4.2 kg baby and an 18-hour oxytocin induction make atony likely.

parts.label: Actions in order
parts.criteria: Fundal massage at once; empty the bladder; increase oxytocin per protocol; weigh the loss; second large-bore IV; activate the hemorrhage team with numbers; does not give methylergonovine because of her hypertension; gives the ordered carboprost (watching for bronchospasm) and tranexamic acid within 3 hours of birth.
parts.modelAnswer: Massage the fundus now, empty her bladder, increase the oxytocin per protocol and weigh everything. Put in a second large-bore IV. Activate the hemorrhage team with the QBL, the trend and what I've done. Not methylergonovine: she is hypertensive. Give the ordered carboprost, watching her breathing, and tranexamic acid, which works only if given within 3 hours of birth.

noProgress.rationale: A postpartum hemorrhage still uncontrolled 90 minutes later is ongoing bleeding past the point of a 1000 mL hemorrhage, so this case calls it harm.

metherHarm.label: Bleeding treated, but a contraindicated drug given
metherHarm.narrative: {timeAt(controlledAt)|clock}: the bleeding is controlled at a QBL of {round(loss / 10) * 10} mL, but methylergonovine went into a client who was already hypertensive. Her BP climbed to the 180s over 110s with a pounding headache, the warning signs of a stroke or seizure that the drug's label lists. Methylergonovine is contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia: leave it in the kit and use oxytocin, carboprost (no asthma) and tranexamic acid.

expertPath.text: Fundus boggy and pushed to the right, bladder full: massage now, increase the oxytocin per protocol, catheterize.
Weigh everything: QBL past 500 mL and rising. Second large-bore IV.
Activate the hemorrhage team with the QBL, the trend, the HR and what you have done. Leave methylergonovine in the kit: she is hypertensive.
Team orders carboprost and tranexamic acid: give both, watching her breathing. The uterus firms.

shock.headline: Hemorrhagic shock
shock.body: Find when the loss was first weighed, when the bladder was emptied, and when the team was called with numbers. A normal BP after birth does not mean the loss is small.

controlled.headline: Measured, treated, escalated
controlled.body: You weighed the loss, treated the atony in the right order, kept the contraindicated drug in the kit and brought the team early. That is the expert path.

controlledLate.headline: Controlled, by a slower or riskier route
controlledLate.body: Check how the loss was measured, how long until the call with numbers, whether the bladder was emptied, and whether methylergonovine was given despite her hypertension.

time_up.headline: Still bleeding
time_up.body: Atony needs massage, an empty bladder, more uterotonic and the team. When the first steps do not hold, escalate.

scoring.modelReasoning: A boggy fundus displaced above the umbilicus and to one side, heavy bleeding with clots and a loss passing 500 mL an hour after a big baby and a long oxytocin induction is a postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony until proven otherwise. Measure it by weighing (eyeball estimates undercount), and do not be reassured by a normal BP: postpartum women mask loss until late, and a rising HR comes first. Massage the fundus, empty the bladder so the uterus can contract, increase the oxytocin per protocol, add a large-bore IV, and activate the hemorrhage team with numbers. Methylergonovine is contraindicated with hypertension; carboprost needs care with asthma; tranexamic acid helps only within 3 hours of birth.

cathQ.ask: While the catheter drains: why does a full bladder matter here?

choices.label: It pushes the uterus up and aside and keeps it from contracting

cathQ.explain: A full bladder displaces the uterus and stops it contracting well, so a boggy, displaced fundus calls for emptying the bladder along with massage.
